topics.name: Conditional Probability and the Multiplication Theorem
topics.summary: Conditional probability asks: given that event B has already happened, what is the chance that A also happens? It is written \( P(A|B) \) and defined as \( \dfrac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)} \), where B (the event already known to have occurred) always sits in the denominator. A very common mistake is swapping this — computing \( P(B|A) \) when \( P(A|B) \) was asked, or vice versa; these two quantities are generally different. The multiplication theorem rearranges the same definition to find joint probabilities: \( P(A \cap B) = P(A) \cdot P(B|A) \), which is especially useful for sequential experiments like drawing cards or balls without replacement, where each draw changes the probabilities for the next. Students should get comfortable reducing a sample space once an event is known to have occurred, and chaining several conditional probabilities together for multi-step draws.
key_formulas: \( P(A \cap B) = P(A) \cdot P(B|A) = P(B) \cdot P(A|B) \)
\( P(A \cap B \cap C) = P(A) \cdot P(B|A) \cdot P(C|A \cap B) \)
topics.worked_example: A bag has 5 red and 3 blue balls. Two are drawn one after another without replacement. Find \( P(\text{both red}) \). By the multiplication theorem, \( P(\text{both red}) = P(\text{1st red}) \cdot P(\text{2nd red}|\text{1st red}) = \dfrac{5}{8} \times \dfrac{4}{7} = \dfrac{5}{14} \).
common_mistakes: Swapping which event is 'given' — computing \( P(B|A) \) instead of \( P(A|B) \)
Forgetting to update the sample space (and counts) after each draw without replacement
Using \( P(A \cap B) \) itself as the final answer instead of dividing by \( P(B) \)

topics.name: Independent Events and the Theorem of Total Probability
topics.summary: Two events are independent when knowing one occurred tells you nothing about the other: \( P(A \cap B) = P(A) \cdot P(B) \). This is completely different from being mutually exclusive, where \( P(A \cap B) = 0 \) — independent events with positive probability can never be mutually exclusive, and this distinction drives many exam traps, including which addition rule to use for \( P(A \cup B) \). The Theorem of Total Probability handles situations built from a partition \( E_1, E_2, \ldots, E_n \) of the sample space (mutually exclusive, exhaustive branches, such as choosing one of several bags or machines): \( P(A) = \sum_i P(E_i) \cdot P(A|E_i) \). Every branch of the partition must be included in the sum — leaving one out is a very common error. This chapter blends numeric independence checks, 'at least one' style problems using complements, and multi-branch total probability setups.
key_formulas: Independent union: \( P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A)P(B) \)
Total Probability: \( P(A) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} P(E_i)\,P(A|E_i) \), for a partition \( E_1,\ldots,E_n \)
topics.worked_example: Bag I has 3 red, 2 white balls; Bag II has 4 red, 1 white ball. A bag is chosen at random and a ball drawn. Find \( P(\text{red}) \). \( P(\text{red}) = \dfrac{1}{2}\cdot\dfrac{3}{5} + \dfrac{1}{2}\cdot\dfrac{4}{5} = \dfrac{3}{10}+\dfrac{4}{10} = \dfrac{7}{10} \).
common_mistakes: Confusing independence (\( P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B) \)) with mutual exclusivity (\( P(A\cap B)=0 \))
Using the mutually-exclusive addition rule \( P(A)+P(B) \) for independent events instead of \( P(A)+P(B)-P(A)P(B) \)
Leaving one branch out of the total-probability sum, especially with 3-way partitions

topics.name: Bayes' Theorem
topics.summary: Bayes' Theorem reverses a conditional probability: given that A has occurred, what's the probability it came from a particular branch \( E_i \) of a partition? It builds directly on the Theorem of Total Probability, reusing the same total-probability sum as its denominator: \( P(E_i|A) = \dfrac{P(E_i)P(A|E_i)}{\sum_j P(E_j)P(A|E_j)} \). A frequent error is reporting just the numerator term (forgetting to divide by the total), or mismatching which branch's prior and likelihood go together in the numerator. Bayes' theorem is also the tool behind the classic 'base-rate neglect' trap: when an event is rare, even a fairly accurate test can still give a surprisingly low posterior probability, because most positive results come from the much larger group of people who don't actually have the rare condition. This chapter builds comfort with correctly identifying the partition, computing every branch's contribution, and not confusing the reversed conditional with the original one.
key_formulas: Denominator = Total Probability of A across the whole partition
topics.worked_example: Urn I has 3 red, 2 black; Urn II has 2 red, 4 black; a red ball is drawn. Find \( P(\text{Urn I}|\text{red}) \). \( P(\text{red}) = \dfrac{1}{2}\cdot\dfrac{3}{5}+\dfrac{1}{2}\cdot\dfrac{1}{3} = \dfrac{7}{15} \); so \( P(\text{Urn I}|\text{red}) = \dfrac{3/10}{7/15} = \dfrac{9}{14} \).
common_mistakes: Reporting the Bayes' numerator alone, forgetting to divide by the total probability
Leaving a branch out of the denominator's sum (an incomplete partition)
Confusing the reversed posterior \( P(E_i|A) \) with the given conditional \( P(A|E_i) \), especially with rare-event 'base-rate neglect' problems

topics.name: Random Variables and Probability Distributions: Mean and Variance
topics.summary: A random variable X assigns a number to each outcome of an experiment, along with a probability distribution \( P(X=x_i)=p_i \) that must be non-negative and sum to exactly 1. The mean (expectation) \( E(X) = \sum x_i p_i \) is the long-run average value, while the variance \( \text{Var}(X) = E(X^2) - [E(X)]^2 \) measures how spread out the distribution is — note the order: 'mean of the square' minus 'square of the mean', never the other way round. Common setups include coin-toss counts, sums from small numbered tickets, and drawing without replacement from a small bag (a 'hypergeometric-style' distribution, which is just basic \( ^nC_r \) counting, not named explicitly in this course). Students should be comfortable building a full distribution table from a word problem, computing both \( E(X) \) and \( E(X^2) \) before combining them, and applying the linear-transformation rule \( E(aX+b) = aE(X)+b \).
topics.worked_example: For X = number of heads in two tosses of a fair coin, \( P(0)=\dfrac{1}{4},P(1)=\dfrac{1}{2},P(2)=\dfrac{1}{4} \). \( E(X) = 0(\tfrac14)+1(\tfrac12)+2(\tfrac14)=1 \), \( E(X^2)=0(\tfrac14)+1(\tfrac12)+4(\tfrac14)=\tfrac32 \), so \( \text{Var}(X)=\tfrac32-1=\tfrac12 \).
common_mistakes: Reporting \( E(X^2) \) itself as the variance, forgetting to subtract \( [E(X)]^2 \)
Mismatching each value of X with the wrong probability when computing the weighted sum
Treating a single probability in the table (like \( P(X=1) \)) as if it were the mean, instead of computing the full weighted sum

topics.name: Bernoulli Trials and the Binomial Distribution
topics.summary: A sequence of Bernoulli trials consists of repeated, independent trials, each with exactly two outcomes (success/failure) and the same probability of success \( p \) every time (with \( q=1-p \)). The binomial distribution gives the probability of exactly \( r \) successes in \( n \) trials: \( P(X=r) = {}^nC_r\,p^r q^{n-r} \), and its mean and variance have simple closed forms: \( E(X)=np \) and \( \text{Var}(X)=npq \). The most common exam traps involve mixing up \( p \) and \( q \) (or their exponents) inside the formula, and confusing the variance formula \( npq \) with the mean formula \( np \). 'At least one' and 'at most' problems are usually easiest to solve using the complement rule rather than summing every case directly. This course keeps \( n \) small (at most 8) and probabilities as simple fractions, staying within basic drawing-with-replacement-style experiments — coins, dice, and simple defect rates.
topics.worked_example: A biased coin shows heads with probability \( \dfrac{2}{3} \), tossed 4 times. Find \( P(\text{exactly 3 heads}) \). \( P(X=3) = {}^4C_3\left(\dfrac{2}{3}\right)^3\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right)^1 = 4\times\dfrac{8}{27}\times\dfrac{1}{3}=\dfrac{32}{81} \).
common_mistakes: Swapping the exponents of p and q, applying the success probability to the failure count or vice versa
Using the variance formula \( npq \) when the mean \( np \) was asked for, or vice versa
Omitting the binomial coefficient \( ^nC_r \) entirely, or using the wrong value of r
